title: Péter Magyar Sworn in as Prime Minister of Hungary — 16 Years of Orbán Rule End on Europe Day
detail: On May 9, 2026 — Europe Day — the Hungarian National Assembly held its inaugural session beginning at 10:00 AM at the Budapest Parliament building. President Tamás Sulyok presided over the swearing-in ceremony. Magyar was elected Prime Minister by 140 votes in favour, 54 against, and 1 abstention. His 15-member cabinet (minus the vacant Justice Ministry) was simultaneously sworn in. Ágnes Forsthoffer of the Tisza Party was elected as the new Speaker of the National Assembly in a landmark vote — the first non-Fidesz Speaker since 2010. Thousands of supporters gathered at Kossuth Square outside parliament, waving Hungarian and EU flags, as the transition was broadcast live across Europe. Viktor Orbán, breaking a 36-year tradition, did not attend the inaugural session and gave no speech — an unusually total break with parliamentary decorum. Foreign leaders including several EU heads of government sent congratulatory messages.

media.caption: Péter Magyar sworn in as Prime Minister of Hungary in the National Assembly on May 9, Europe Day
Supporters celebrate Magyar's swearing-in outside Budapest Parliament

title: EU Flag Restored to Hungarian Parliament Building — Speaker Forsthoffer's First Act After 12 Years
detail: In a powerful symbolic gesture, newly elected Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer ordered the restoration of the EU flag to the facade of the Hungarian Parliament building as her first official act after being elected Speaker on May 9. The EU flag had been removed by Viktor Orbán's government approximately 12 years earlier as part of his campaign against Brussels interference in Hungarian sovereignty. The re-hoisting of the EU flag was broadcast live and received widespread international coverage, with EU leaders and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen welcoming the move as a signal of Hungary's return to the European family. Crowds gathered outside parliament cheered as the flag was raised alongside the Hungarian tricolor. The gesture also carried significance on Europe Day — the anniversary of the Schuman Declaration of May 9, 1950 — deliberatly chosen by Magyar as the inauguration date.

media.caption: EU flag restored to the Hungarian Parliament facade on May 9 after approximately 12 years' absence

title: Magyar Demands President Sulyok Resign by May 31 — First Major Constitutional Confrontation
detail: In his inaugural speech as Prime Minister, Péter Magyar called on President Tamás Sulyok to resign from his position by May 31, 2026. Magyar cited Sulyok's failure to resist democratic backsliding under Orbán, his role as former Constitutional Court President when Fidesz used that institution to insulate its policies from judicial review, and alleged abuses at state-run children's homes that Sulyok had not adequately investigated during his presidency. Sulyok said he would 'consider' the demand but gave no commitment to resign. Fidesz immediately mobilized in defense of Sulyok, with Gergely Gulyás — now parliamentary opposition leader — condemning Magyar's demand as an attempt to 'weaponize political pressure against an independent constitutional institution.' Viktor Orbán personally signed a pro-Sulyok counter-petition circulated by Fidesz. The confrontation opened the first major constitutional question of the post-Orbán era: what happens if the President refuses to comply, given his term does not expire until 2029.

media.caption: Magyar's demand that President Sulyok resign opened the first major constitutional confrontation of the post-Orbán era

title: Magyar Government Issues First Decree — Office for Investigation of Corruption Crimes Established
detail: Among the first acts of the Magyar government after its inauguration on May 9 was a decree establishing a dedicated Office for Investigation of Corruption Crimes (OICC). The new body is designed to be independent of the Interior Ministry and existing police structures — which critics noted had been politicized under Orbán — and will have the authority to investigate public corruption, including cases involving former government officials, oligarchs connected to Fidesz, and misuse of EU funds. The creation of the OICC is a key milestone on the roadmap agreed with the European Commission to unlock €17B in frozen EU funds. Magyar framed the institution as Hungary's domestic equivalent of the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO), which Hungary had refused to join under Orbán. Hungary's formal application to join EPPO was simultaneously submitted as a government resolution on May 9.

media.caption: Magyar government's first decree establishes an anti-corruption office and submits Hungary's EPPO membership application
